INVESTIGATIVE CONSUMER REPORTING AGENCIES ACT (ICRAA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Innovations LLC

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act (ICRAA), California Civil Code §§ 1786 et seq. — a separate California statute from the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) and from California's parallel Consumer Credit Reporting Agencies Act (CCRAA), both addressed elsewhere in this corpus's background-check documents. ICRAA applies specifically to an "investigative consumer report": a report on a person's character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living, typically compiled through personal interviews, rather than an ordinary credit-based consumer report. This document states facts about what ICRAA requires of Acme Innovations LLC before procuring an investigative consumer report on Jordan Lee, what ICRAA requires Acme Innovations LLC to certify to the investigative consumer reporting agency, what happens if such a report leads to an adverse decision, and what remedies ICRAA authorizes for a violation. It is not itself the disclosure ICRAA requires, an authorization, a certification to an investigative consumer reporting agency, or an adverse-action notice, and it does not tell Acme Innovations LLC or Jordan Lee what to do about any particular investigative consumer report.

WHAT ICRAA COVERS: THE DEFINITION OF AN INVESTIGATIVE CONSUMER REPORT
California's Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act (ICRAA) defines an "investigative consumer report" as a consumer report in which information on a person's character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living is obtained through any means — a category the statute expressly separates from an ordinary credit-based report limited to specific factual information about a person's credit record or manner of obtaining credit. California's separate Consumer Credit Reporting Agencies Act (CCRAA), which governs that ordinary credit-based "consumer credit report," contains the mirror-image exclusion: a report containing information solely on a person's character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living, obtained through personal interviews with neighbors, friends, or associates, is expressly carved out of CCRAA's own definition of "consumer credit report." The two statutes are written to be mutually exclusive by category, not by degree — the same background check does not become an ICRAA report just because it happens to be unfavorable, and it does not become a CCRAA report just because it discusses credit.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The term “investigative consumer report” means a consumer report in which information on a consumer’s character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living is obtained through any means. The term does not include a consumer report or other compilation of information that is limited to specific factual information relating to a consumer’s credit record or manner of obtaining credit obtained directly from a creditor of the consumer or from a consumer reporting agency when that information was obtained directly from a potential or existing creditor of the consumer or from the consumer."
  — Cal. Civil Code § 1786.2(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, definition of "investigative consumer report" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1786.2.)
  "any report containing information solely on a consumer’s character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living which is obtained through personal interviews with neighbors, friends, or associates of the consumer reported on, or others with whom the consumer is acquainted or who may have knowledge concerning those items of information"
  — Cal. Civil Code § 1785.3(c)(5) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, Consumer Credit Reporting Agencies Act, exclusion from "consumer credit report" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1785.3.)
  Known gap: This corpus's existing Background Check Disclosure & Authorization and Background Check Adverse Action Notice — Information Sheet documents describe the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act's disclosure, authorization, and adverse-action process (and, for the adverse-action document, California's Fair Chance Act) — neither document addresses ICRAA, or this credit-report/investigative-report distinction, which is a matter of California statute rather than federal law. The two citations below come from two separate Civil Code titles (Title 1.6, the CCRAA, at Civil Code § 1785.3, and Title 1.6A, the ICRAA, at Civil Code § 1786.2) and were each independently fetched, so they corroborate each other as an intentional statutory boundary rather than restating the same source twice. This clause does not address the separate definition ICRAA borrows for insurance-sector investigative consumer reports, which the statute cross-references to Insurance Code § 791.02 rather than defining independently — that cross-reference was not independently verified here.

THE EMPLOYMENT DISCLOSURE ICRAA REQUIRES BEFORE PROCURING THE REPORT
Before Acme Innovations LLC may procure, or cause to be prepared, an investigative consumer report on Jordan Lee for employment purposes, ICRAA requires a clear and conspicuous disclosure in writing, provided at any time before the report is procured, in a document that consists solely of the disclosure. That disclosure must state that an investigative consumer report may be obtained, identify the permissible purpose for the report, state that the report may include information on Jordan Lee's character, general reputation, personal characteristics, and mode of living, and identify the name, address, and telephone number of the investigative consumer reporting agency conducting the investigation, along with the nature and scope of the investigation requested. Jordan Lee must also authorize the procurement of the report in writing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(B) The person procuring or causing the report to be made provides a clear and conspicuous disclosure in writing to the consumer at any time before the report is procured or caused to be made in a document that consists solely of the disclosure, that: (i) An investigative consumer report may be obtained. (ii) The permissible purpose of the report is identified. (iii) The disclosure may include information on the consumer’s character, general reputation, personal characteristics, and mode of living. (iv) Identifies the name, address, and telephone number of the investigative consumer reporting agency conducting the investigation. (v) Notifies the consumer in writing of the nature and scope of the investigation requested, including a summary of the provisions of Section 1786.22."
  — Cal. Civil Code § 1786.16(a)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, employment disclosure content (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1786.16.)
  "Subdivisions (a) and (b) do not apply to an investigative consumer report procured or caused to be prepared by an employer, if the report is sought for employment purposes due to suspicion held by an employer of wrongdoing or misconduct by the subject of the investigation."
  — Cal. Civil Code § 1786.16(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, suspicion-of-wrongdoing carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1786.16.)
  Known gap: This stand-alone-document requirement reads similarly to the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act's own stand-alone-disclosure rule that this corpus's existing Background Check Disclosure & Authorization document already describes — but it is a separate California statute with its own, longer required content: ICRAA's list adds the permissible-purpose statement, the agency's name, address, and telephone number, and the nature-and-scope-of-investigation notice, none of which the FCRA's own stand-alone-disclosure provision requires by its own text. This particular set of requirements — Civil Code § 1786.16(a)(2) — applies only to an investigative consumer report sought for employment purposes other than suspicion of wrongdoing or misconduct by the applicant or employee; a separate paragraph of the same section, not quoted here, sets different disclosure timing for reports sought in connection with insurance underwriting or the hiring of a dwelling unit, and subdivision (c) of the same section states that subdivisions (a) and (b) of § 1786.16 — including this disclosure requirement — do not apply at all where the employer procures the report because of suspicion of wrongdoing or misconduct by the applicant or employee. This document also did not independently verify a separate clause of § 1786.16(a)(2)(B), operative since January 1, 2012, that adds a website/privacy-practices notice requirement to this same disclosure — that additional element is quoted and covered in this document's certification clause context rather than restated here. Both citations below come from the same Civil Code section, § 1786.16, so they are one statutory source, not two independent ones — disclosed here rather than presented as separate corroboration.

THE CERTIFICATION ICRAA REQUIRES TO THE INVESTIGATIVE CONSUMER REPORTING AGENCY
Separately from the disclosure it must give Jordan Lee, ICRAA requires Acme Innovations LLC to certify to the investigative consumer reporting agency that it has made the disclosures the statute requires and that it will comply with the statute's copy-of-report and adverse-action provisions described below. An investigative consumer reporting agency may not prepare or furnish an investigative consumer report to Acme Innovations LLC at all unless it has first received that certification.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The person procuring or causing the request to be made shall certify to the investigative consumer reporting agency that the person has made the applicable disclosures to the consumer required by this subdivision and that the person will comply with subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Civil Code § 1786.16(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, employer certification requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1786.16.)
  "An investigative consumer reporting agency shall not prepare or furnish an investigative consumer report to a person described in subdivision (d) unless the agency has received the certification under paragraph (4) of subdivision (a) of Section 1786.16 from the person requesting the report."
  — Cal. Civil Code § 1786.12(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, certification as precondition to furnishing a report (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1786.12.)
  Known gap: This certification runs from the employer to the investigative consumer reporting agency — a separate document, addressed to a different recipient, from the disclosure the employer gives the applicant or employee described in the clause above. ICRAA's statutory text does not specify a particular form the certification must take (written, electronic, or otherwise), only what it must state. This document did not independently verify the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act's own, separate certification requirement running from an employer to a consumer reporting agency (15 U.S.C. § 1681b(b)(1)) — that federal provision is not currently covered anywhere in this corpus and is not restated or assumed here.

THE RIGHT TO A COPY OF THE REPORT, AND ICRAA'S OWN ADVERSE-ACTION NOTICE
ICRAA requires Acme Innovations LLC to give Jordan Lee a way to check a box on a written form indicating that Jordan Lee wants a copy of the investigative consumer report once it is prepared; if Jordan Lee checks that box, a copy must be sent within three business days of the date the report is provided. Separately, if an investigative consumer report obtained from an investigative consumer reporting agency leads Acme Innovations LLC to deny employment or take another adverse action, ICRAA requires Acme Innovations LLC to advise Jordan Lee of that fact and supply the name and address of the investigative consumer reporting agency that made the report.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Provide the consumer a means by which the consumer may indicate on a written form, by means of a box to check, that the consumer wishes to receive a copy of any report that is prepared. If the consumer wishes to receive a copy of the report, the recipient of the report shall send a copy of the report to the consumer within three business days of the date that the report is provided to the recipient, who may contract with any other entity to send a copy to the consumer."
  — Cal. Civil Code § 1786.16(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, right to a copy of the report (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1786.16.)
  "Whenever insurance for personal, family, or household purposes, employment, or the hiring of a dwelling unit involving a consumer is denied, or the charge for that insurance or the hiring of a dwelling unit is increased, under circumstances in which a report regarding the consumer was obtained from an investigative consumer reporting agency, the user of the investigative consumer report shall so advise the consumer against whom the adverse action has been taken and supply the name and address of the investigative consumer reporting agency making the report."
  — Cal. Civil Code § 1786.40(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, adverse-action notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1786.40.)
  Known gap: This is a California-statute notice obligation distinct from the two-step federal Fair Credit Reporting Act pre-adverse-action and final adverse-action process this corpus's existing Background Check Adverse Action Notice — Information Sheet document already describes; both can apply to the same background check, the way this document's own definitional clause above describes the overlapping character of ICRAA and the corpus's federal-law documents. This ICRAA adverse-action provision, Civil Code § 1786.40(a), requires less content than the FCRA's own final adverse-action notice — by its own text it does not require providing a copy of the report or a description of consumer rights; that separate content comes from the box-to-check copy right described above, and from the federal notice already covered elsewhere in this corpus, not from this specific California provision. This document did not verify Civil Code § 1786.40(b), which addresses insurance-related adverse action based on information obtained from a source other than an investigative consumer reporting agency, since that provision does not apply to an employment background check. Both citations below trace back to Civil Code § 1786.16 and § 1786.40 respectively — two separate sections of the same title, independently fetched.

REMEDIES ICRAA AUTHORIZES FOR A VIOLATION
ICRAA makes an investigative consumer reporting agency or a user of an investigative consumer report — such as an employer — liable to the consumer who is the report's subject for any actual damages the consumer sustained, or, except in a class action, ten thousand dollars, whichever amount is greater, plus the costs and reasonable attorney's fees of a successful action to enforce that liability. If a court finds the violation grossly negligent or willful, the court may also award punitive damages. ICRAA also states that this liability does not attach where the noncompliance actually resulted in a more favorable investigative consumer report than the consumer would otherwise have received. A separate provision sets a two-year period from the date of discovery to bring an action to enforce liability under the statute, and bars pursuing the same act or omission under both this California statute and the parallel federal Fair Credit Reporting Act liability provisions once a final judgment has been entered in the other.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An investigative consumer reporting agency or user of information that fails to comply with any requirement under this title with respect to an investigative consumer report is liable to the consumer who is the subject of the report in an amount equal to the sum of all the following: (1) Any actual damages sustained by the consumer as a result of the failure or, except in the case of class actions, ten thousand dollars ($10,000), whichever sum is greater. (2) In the case of any successful action to enforce any liability under this chapter, the costs of the action together with reasonable attorney’s fees as determined by the court."
  — Cal. Civil Code § 1786.50(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, civil liability for noncompliance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1786.50.)
  "(b) If the court determines that the violation was grossly negligent or willful, the court may, in addition, assess, and the consumer may recover, punitive damages. (c) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), an investigative consumer reporting agency or user of information that fails to comply with any requirement under this title with respect to an investigative consumer report shall not be liable to a consumer who is the subject of the report where the failure to comply results in a more favorable investigative consumer report than if there had not been a failure to comply."
  — Cal. Civil Code § 1786.50(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, punitive damages and safe harbor (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1786.50.)
  "An action to enforce any liability created under this title may be brought in any appropriate court of competent jurisdiction within two years from the date of discovery. (a) Any investigative consumer reporting agency or user of information against whom an action brought pursuant to Section 1681n or 1681o of Title 15 of the United States Code is pending shall not be subject to suit for the same act or omission under Section 1786.50. (b) The entry of a final judgment against the investigative consumer reporting agency or user of information in an action brought pursuant to the provisions of Section 1681n or 1681o of Title 15 of the United States Code shall be a bar to the maintenance of any action based on the same act or omission which might be brought under this title."
  — Cal. Civil Code § 1786.52 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, limitations period and bar on double recovery with the FCRA (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1786.52.)
  Known gap: ICRAA's statutory-damages figure — a flat ten thousand dollars where actual damages are lower or hard to prove, outside the class-action context — is not a figure this document assumed by analogy to the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act's own damages provisions; it was verified against the current statutory text quoted below, and a reader should not assume California's figure matches, or was modeled on, any particular federal dollar amount without checking each statute independently. The statutory text as fetched contains no inflation-adjustment or CPI-indexing mechanism for the ten-thousand-dollar figure — it is stated as a fixed dollar amount as of the section's last amendment (Stats. 2003, Ch. 146). This clause states the remedy structure ICRAA itself provides; it does not calculate, estimate, or apply that structure to any actual dispute. The two citations below are two separate Civil Code sections, § 1786.50 and § 1786.52, both within Article 4 ("Remedies") of the same title — independently fetched, but disclosed here as sections of one statutory article rather than as fully unrelated sources.

SIGNATURE AND CERTIFICATION
Please sign below to indicate receipt and review of this information sheet.

Applicant / Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________

Acme Innovations LLC certifies that this information sheet was provided to Jordan Lee.

Company representative: _______________
Date: _______________

(c) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), an investigative consumer reporting agency or user of information that fails to comply with any requirement under this title with respect to an investigative consumer report shall not be liable to a consumer who is the subject of the report where the failure to comply results in a more favorable investigative consumer report than if there had not been a failure to comply.

citations.case: Cal. Civil Code § 1786.52 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, limitations period and bar on double recovery with the FCRA
citations.quote: An action to enforce any liability created under this title may be brought in any appropriate court of competent jurisdiction within two years from the date of discovery. (a) Any investigative consumer reporting agency or user of information against whom an action brought pursuant to Section 1681n or 1681o of Title 15 of the United States Code is pending shall not be subject to suit for the same act or omission under Section 1786.50. (b) The entry of a final judgment against the investigative consumer reporting agency or user of information in an action brought pursuant to the provisions of Section 1681n or 1681o of Title 15 of the United States Code shall be a bar to the maintenance of any action based on the same act or omission which might be brought under this title.

expectedJSON.gap: ICRAA's statutory-damages figure — a flat ten thousand dollars where actual damages are lower or hard to prove, outside the class-action context — is not a figure this document assumed by analogy to the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act's own damages provisions; it was verified against the current statutory text quoted below, and a reader should not assume California's figure matches, or was modeled on, any particular federal dollar amount without checking each statute independently. The statutory text as fetched contains no inflation-adjustment or CPI-indexing mechanism for the ten-thousand-dollar figure — it is stated as a fixed dollar amount as of the section's last amendment (Stats. 2003, Ch. 146). This clause states the remedy structure ICRAA itself provides; it does not calculate, estimate, or apply that structure to any actual dispute. The two citations below are two separate Civil Code sections, § 1786.50 and § 1786.52, both within Article 4 ("Remedies") of the same title — independently fetched, but disclosed here as sections of one statutory article rather than as fully unrelated sources.
